sections.body: **Content note:** this page discusses abuse, forced treatment, restraint and deaths in psychiatric hospitals. [Where to report abuse is listed below.](#kop-ri-report)

sections.label: What this page covers
sections.heading: What this page covers
sections.body:
This page is about psychiatric hospitals and psych wards: free-standing psychiatric hospitals, the psychiatric units of general hospitals, and state and county hospitals, for adults and for young people. It covers them whether or not a hospital is also part of the troubled teen industry. Most stays are short, often after a crisis and often involuntary.

Many youth programs we track are on a psychiatric hospital's campus, carry its name and its owner, or are a unit inside the hospital. Medicaid's inpatient psychiatric benefit for people under 21 pays psychiatric hospitals, the psychiatric programs of general hospitals and accredited residential psychiatric facilities under the same rule.[^1] About 60 programs in our records are named for a hospital or one of its units, among them Cedar Crest Hospital & RTC in Texas, Hampstead Hospital & RTC in New Hampshire, West Oaks Hospital PRTF in Texas and the adolescent programs of River Park Hospital in West Virginia.[^2] Those residential treatment centers and psychiatric residential treatment facilities (PRTFs) are in [our directory](/tti-program-index/). This page is about the hospitals and wards themselves.

The largest for-profit chains run both, and the same practices and the same pressure to fill beds are documented in both. They also share a history, told below and in our [history pages](/history/). We are not the experts on psychiatric hospitals. The organizations listed below are, and many of them are run by people who have been hospitalized themselves.

sections.label: What the industry is
sections.heading: What psychiatric hospitals are
sections.body:
Inpatient psychiatric care happens in three kinds of place: free-standing psychiatric hospitals, psychiatric units inside general hospitals (often called psych wards), and state and county hospitals. When Medicare began in 1965, state and local hospitals provided most of this care. In 2023, only 4 percent of Medicare-covered psychiatric hospital days were in government-run free-standing hospitals, and 35 percent were in privately owned ones.[^3] The rest were in general hospital units.

Medicare counted 1,430 certified inpatient psychiatric facilities in fiscal year 2024, down from 1,610 in 2019. Of these, 59 percent were units inside general hospitals. Over a quarter were free-standing for-profit hospitals, up from about one-fifth in 2019.[^4] A 2024 national survey of treatment facilities counted 60,201 inpatient mental health beds for all ages.[^5]

Medicaid, Medicare, private insurance and state budgets pay for this care. Acadia Healthcare, one of the two largest for-profit chains, received 57.7 percent of its 2025 revenue from Medicaid and 14.3 percent from Medicare.[^6]

Many admissions are involuntary. States allow emergency holds for evaluation and court-ordered commitment, under rules and time limits that differ from state to state, and there is no national count. A study published in *Psychiatric Services* in 2020 used data from 24 states with 52 percent of the population and found 357 emergency involuntary detentions per 100,000 people in 2014, about 591,000 detentions in those states alone. In 22 states with data for 2012 to 2016, the detention rate rose 13 percent while the population grew 4 percent.[^7]

sections.label: History
sections.heading: Where psychiatric hospitals and the TTI came from
sections.body:
### Asylums and "insanity in children"

The psychiatric hospital began as the asylum, and the asylum held children. England's Lunacy Act of 1845 set up a commission to inspect every asylum, public and private, wrote into law who counted as a "lunatic" or an "idiot," and gave magistrates and Poor Law officials more power to take people from their families and place them in asylums, children with intellectual disabilities or behavioral issues among them. In 1892 the American Medico-Psychological Association, forerunner of the American Psychiatric Association, recognized insanity in children as a medical category, which legitimized more asylum space for children. In 1896 Lightner Witmer opened the first U.S. child psychiatric clinic, at the University of Pennsylvania, though early child psychology focused more on correcting children than supporting them. Eugenics taught that mental illness was hereditary and that children with mental disorders were a risk to society; it fed institutionalization and forced sterilization, upheld by the Supreme Court in *Buck v. Bell* (1927).[^8]

### Psychiatry moves into children's institutions

In 1914 the National Committee for Mental Hygiene surveyed institutions across the country, reformatories and training schools included, starting formal psychiatric oversight of juvenile justice: IQ tests, diagnostic labels and court clinics. In 1930 the White House Conference on Child Health and Protection declared delinquent acts to be symptoms of psychological problems rather than simple lawbreaking.[^9] From then on a troublesome child was a child who needed treatment, for as long as the experts said.[^10]

The residential treatment center came out of the psychiatric hospital. In 1926 the Menninger Clinic in Topeka, Kansas, opened the Southard School as its children's division. Meant at first for children with intellectual disabilities, it became a prototype for psychoanalytic residential treatment centers.[^8]

### The hospital as a therapeutic community

Many group methods later used on teenagers were first tried on psychiatric patients. At Northfield Military Hospital in England, Wilfred Bion and John Rickman brought group psychotherapy into a military psychiatric hospital (1942 to 1944). Tom Main, who visited Northfield, coined the term "therapeutic community" in 1946 in a *Lancet* paper, "The Hospital as a Therapeutic Institution," for a hospital run through democratic participation and shared responsibility. Maxwell Jones and others formalized the democratic therapeutic community for psychiatric patients at Henderson Hospital in 1961 and 1962.[^11]

In the United States, Synanon (1958) grew out of its founder's part in an LSD study funded by the National Institute of Mental Health. Daytop Village (1964), co-founded by psychiatrist Daniel Casriel with an NIMH grant, fused Synanon's model with professional therapy, and psychiatrist Gerald Davidson co-founded Elan School (1971). The Seed, CEDU and Straight, Inc. carried Synanon's methods into programs for teenagers.[^10]

### Deinstitutionalization and private money

The Community Mental Health Act of 1963 funded community centers meant to replace the large institutions; underfunding and lack of follow-through left gaps that private facilities filled.[^8] The act also placed addiction under the heading of mental illness.[^12] After Medicaid and Medicare (1965), public money could follow a child into a private residential placement, and from the 1960s to the 1980s poor children were moved from orphanages to psychiatric or behavioral facilities.[^13]

### The hospital chains

For-profit psychiatric hospital chains grew alongside the youth programs, and often owned both. Charter Behavioral Health Systems, established in 1979, bought the original campus of Provo Canyon School in 1986 and owned it for 14 years. In 1982 former Charter Medical executives bought the Brown Schools, a Texas youth treatment company founded in 1940, renamed it Healthcare International and added psychiatric hospitals.[^14] In 1993 Robert Lichfield, who had started as a dorm parent at Provo Canyon School and later founded WWASP, took over the management of Brightway Adolescent Hospital in St. George, Utah. Health officials said the hospital promptly began sending young people to tough-love behavior programs. Its owner ended the agreement and closed the hospital in 1998.[^15]

By 1999 Charter, then the largest private operator of behavioral health facilities in the country, ran 91 hospitals and treated 120,000 inpatients a year, 35,000 of them children and adolescents; that year *60 Minutes II* reported on deaths in restraint at its hospitals (see below).[^14] In 2000, in Chapter 11, Charter sold 11 facilities to Universal Health Services, Provo Canyon School among them.[^16][^17] In 2005 UHS added the Keystone youth programs and five former Brown Schools programs. Acadia Healthcare, formed that year, bought CRC Health Group, owner of Aspen Education Group's teen programs, in 2015.[^14] UHS and Acadia are the companies in the next section.

sections.label: How it is connected to the TTI
sections.heading: How it is connected to the troubled teen industry
sections.body:
### The same companies

Universal Health Services (UHS) runs one of the largest networks of psychiatric hospitals in the country. Its annual report for 2025 lists 182 inpatient behavioral health facilities in the United States, plus 161 in the United Kingdom and 3 in Puerto Rico.[^18] The same list includes psychiatric hospitals and youth programs such as Provo Canyon School and Copper Hills Youth Center in Utah and Oak Plains Academy in Tennessee. In some places a hospital and a residential treatment center share a name: Cedar Ridge Behavioral Hospital and Cedar Ridge Residential Treatment Center in Oklahoma City, and North Star Hospital in Anchorage with the North Star DeBarr and Palmer residential treatment centers.[^18] Our records list 75 programs under [Universal Health Services](/operator/universal-health-services/).

Acadia Healthcare ran 277 behavioral health facilities with over 12,500 beds in 40 states and Puerto Rico at the end of 2025.[^6] Not counting its addiction clinics, about 60 percent are acute psychiatric hospitals and 9 percent are residential treatment centers. The company writes that the children and adolescents in those centers "typically have had multiple prior failed treatment plans," and that stays run from three months to several years.[^6] Our records list 14 programs under [Acadia Healthcare](/operator/acadia-healthcare/).

### The same practices

Federal rules for hospitals forbid restraint or seclusion "imposed as a means of coercion, discipline, convenience, or retaliation by staff."[^19] They count a drug given to manage a patient's behavior, when it is not a standard treatment or dose for the patient's condition, as a restraint, and they require hospitals to report to CMS every death that happens in restraint or seclusion or within 24 hours after it.[^19] Physical restraint, seclusion and drugs used to control behavior are the same practices documented in troubled teen programs.

In 2024 the U.S. Senate Finance Committee published *Warehouses of Neglect* ([our summary](/warehouses-of-neglect/)), a two-year investigation of youth residential treatment run by UHS, Acadia, Devereux and Vivant. It found that these providers "optimize per diems by filling large facilities to capacity and maximize profit by concurrently reducing the number and quality of staff."[^20] Asked whether a child could be chemically restrained and secluded at once, UHS personnel told committee staff "there are no rules preventing doubling or tripling up on a restraint and seclusion." The report notes that the practice is prohibited by federal regulations.[^20] Investigators and reporters have described the same pressure to fill beds in the companies' psychiatric hospitals (see below).

### Providers outside the industry

We keep a separate [list of mental health providers](/mental-health-providers/) outside the troubled teen industry, such as psychiatric units, that use its practices or refer young people to its programs.

sections.label: What investigations found
sections.heading: What investigations have found
sections.body:
- **1998 to 1999, restraint deaths.** The Hartford Courant's 1998 series "Deadly Restraint" counted 142 deaths tied to restraint or seclusion over ten years in psychiatric hospitals, psychiatric wards, group homes and youth residential facilities. A 1999 GAO report requested by members of Congress found that only 15 states had any system to alert their Protection and Advocacy agency to such deaths, identified 24 deaths in fiscal year 1998 from partial records, and said many more may occur. It found that until 1999 no federal rules governed restraint and seclusion in psychiatric hospitals.[^21]
- **1999, Charter.** CBS's *60 Minutes II* report "Unsafe Haven" began with Tristan Sovern, 16, asphyxiated while staff restrained him at a Charter hospital in Greensboro, North Carolina, the third patient in four months to die in restraints in a Charter hospital.[^22] Charter, with 91 hospitals, tried to block the broadcast in court and lost.[^14]
- **2006, unreported deaths.** The HHS Inspector General found that hospitals failed to report to CMS 44 of 104 documented deaths related to restraint and seclusion between August 1999 and December 2004, and that CMS and state survey agencies often did not act on reported deaths in time.[^23]
- **2016, UHS.** A BuzzFeed News investigation, based on interviews with 175 current and former UHS staff, reported that employees at UHS psychiatric hospitals described pressure to fill beds and to keep patients until their insurance ran out. UHS rejected the allegations.[^24]
- **2020, UHS settlement.** UHS and related entities agreed to pay $122 million to settle False Claims Act allegations that from 2006 to 2018 its behavioral health facilities admitted patients who did not need inpatient care, kept them longer than needed, understaffed, and improperly used physical and chemical restraints and seclusion. Liability was not determined. UHS signed a five-year Corporate Integrity Agreement with an independent monitor for its behavioral health division.[^25]
- **2024, Acadia.** A New York Times investigation reported that Acadia held patients against their will when it was not medically necessary, often for financial reasons rather than medical ones, according to more than 50 current and former executives and staff. In at least 12 of the 19 states where Acadia runs psychiatric hospitals, patients, employees and police officers had alerted authorities.[^26] In September 2024 Acadia paid $19.9 million, admitting no liability, to settle a federal investigation of medical necessity, admissions, discharges, length of stay and patient care at several of its facilities.[^6]
- **2024 to 2026, federal investigations of Acadia.** Since September 2024 Acadia has received grand jury subpoenas from the Justice Department's Criminal Division about the admissions, length of stay and billing of its acute psychiatric hospitals, and subpoenas from the SEC. As of its July 2026 quarterly report, the investigations were open, no findings had been made, and the company said it was cooperating.[^27]

sections.label: Where to report abuse
sections.heading: Where to report abuse
sections.body:
- **If someone is in danger now**, call 911. For a mental health crisis, call or text [988](tel:988), the 988 Suicide and Crisis Lifeline, 24 hours a day.
- **Protection and Advocacy agency.** Every state and territory has one. Under the federal PAIMI program they investigate abuse, neglect and rights violations against people with mental illness in public and private facilities, including restraint and seclusion.[^28] Find yours in [NDRN's directory](https://www.ndrn.org/about/ndrn-member-agencies/).
- **State health department.** Hospitals are licensed by the state, and the state survey agency investigates complaints for Medicare and Medicaid. CMS lists [each state's complaint contact](https://www.cms.gov/medicare/health-safety-standards/quality-safety-oversight-general-information/contact-information).
- **The Joint Commission**, if the hospital is accredited by it: [report a safety concern online](https://www.jointcommission.org/en-us/contact-us/report-a-patient-safety-event) or call 1-800-994-6610. You can report anonymously.
- **A death in restraint or seclusion** must be reported by the hospital to CMS. You can also tell the state survey agency and the Protection and Advocacy agency yourself.
- For troubled teen programs, including youth residential treatment run by the same companies, use [our reporting directory](/report-abuse/).

sections.label: Organizations to learn from
sections.heading: Learn from the people who work on this
sections.body:
- [MindFreedom International](https://mindfreedom.org/): A human rights organization in mental health care, with psychiatric survivors among its board and past leaders. It works against forced psychiatric treatment.
- [National Association for Rights Protection and Advocacy (NARPA)](https://www.narpa.org/): Supports people with psychiatric diagnoses in exercising their legal and human rights, and works to end forced treatment.
- [National Empowerment Center](https://power2u.org/): Works with people with lived experience of mental health issues, trauma and extreme states. It keeps directories of peer respites and peer-run warmlines.
- [Wildflower Alliance](https://wildfloweralliance.org/): A grassroots group in Western Massachusetts and online offering peer support, advocacy and training, including peer-run respites.
- [National Disability Rights Network (NDRN)](https://www.ndrn.org/): The national organization of the Protection and Advocacy agencies, the largest providers of legal advocacy for people with disabilities.
- [Bazelon Center for Mental Health Law](https://www.bazelon.org/): A national legal advocacy organization for the civil rights of people with mental disabilities, through lawsuits and policy work.
- [Mad in America](https://www.madinamerica.com/): A publication of the Mad in America Foundation with research news, original journalism and writing by people with lived experience of psychiatric care.

sections.label: Tell us if we got this wrong
sections.heading: Tell us if we got this wrong
sections.body: If you have been hospitalized, work in psychiatric care or advocate in this field, and something on this page is wrong or missing, please [tell us](/contact/). We will change it.
